summary: Publisher NOTIFY failures and bounded-queue overflow now retain one pending gap and retry an explicit resync notification across the existing schema channel, reaching continuously connected remote browser streams.
behavior: One pool NOTIFY in flight, up to 64 compacted first-delivery payloads queued, one pending-gap bit, one resync retry timer; no failed event replay. Each event is at most 7500 bytes before the fixed origin envelope, so retained wire payloads total less than 512 KiB.

If ordinary first delivery fails or queue serialization/size/count cannot be honored, discard pending event payloads and send a small {origin,resync:true} control notification. Repeated changes coalesce into the gap bit while retry is pending.

Retry starts at 1 second and doubles through 2,4,8,16 seconds, capped at 30 seconds; it continues without requiring a later mutation and resets after successful delivery. At most one retry timer/query can be outstanding.
Remote receivers call EventBus.resync on the control message. Schema/channel isolation and same-origin suppression are preserved; local mutation subscribers already saw their own event.

Events arriving while a resync is in flight remain in the bounded queue for first delivery, or set a new pending gap if that queue overflows. Successful control completion cannot erase that later gap.

close clears the first-delivery queue, pending gap and both reconnect/recovery timers. Subsequent publishes do no transport work; late success/failure cannot schedule work; closed listeners ignore incoming notifications.
Existing public API stays unchanged except exported constant RELAY_MAX_QUEUED_EVENTS=64 for bounded behavior tests. Existing compact-event and LISTEN-reconnect behavior are preserved.

coverage: Regression uses actual PgEventRelay, EventBus and workspaceEventStream with fake pg transport; verifies failed send followed by unrelated mutation causes explicit remote SSE resync while all three listener connections remain open.
Same-origin and other-schema subscribers do not receive the recovery resync.
Persistent failures with hundreds of further changes retain one timer and produce only compact control retries at bounded exponential intervals. Recovery works without a fresh event.
Ordinary first-delivery event order survives 65 simultaneous events (one in flight plus 64 queued).
Blocked sends plus hundreds of oversized source events do not dispatch unbounded queries; overflow during in-flight resync produces a second resync.
Close during a pending retry or an in-flight success/failure prevents further query/timer work; pre-existing stream bound/cleanup tests continue passing.
limitations: Synthetic fake-transport tests establish application recovery behavior; no live PostgreSQL, browser, full suite, build, deployed server, git action or external database was used.

Recovery state is intentionally in memory. A publisher process that dies before successfully notifying a pending gap cannot guarantee delivery after its restart; durable revision tracking/outbox remains outside this bounded fix.
One already-started pool query can settle (and may deliver its notification) after close. The database API has no query cancellation primitive; its eventual completion cannot requeue work.

A pool query that never settles prevents further transport attempts on this relay; payload retention stays bounded. Recovery assumes the transport eventually completes or rejects and the process remains running.

Receiving instances must support the new resync control envelope; older deployed versions do not understand it. Coordinate rollout or use the existing browser reconnect invalidation during a mixed-version interval.
Remote control resync invalidates all connected workspaces on that schema rather than retaining an unbounded set of affected workspace IDs. No load/capacity target is asserted.
